flagged.text: According to Czech folk tradition, the evil beings of true noon, called poludnice or generally divé ženy, work their harm chiefly between eleven and twelve o'clock.
flagged.reason: Erben p.183 names the noon beings "poludnice" first and only "generally divé ženy"; the page supports the clause as worded, but whether Erben's noon divé ženy are the same being as Machal's Divozenky rests on the shared name.

Machal p.265 prints "The Divja Zena" without naming a people; Slovenes is read from the Slovenian passage that runs on from p.264, before "The Bulgarian Diva-ta Zena". The same reading carries the native row /names/variants/5/native/0 and the Divja Zena clauses in the Slovenian variant.

grade_rationale.text: Machal records the Wild Women for Czechs (Bohemian Divozenky) and Poles (Polish Dziwozony).
Machal records the Dziwje Zony for the Lusatian Serbs and the Divje Devojke for the Slovenians.

Machal also records the Wild Women for the Bulgarians (Bulgarian Divi-te Zeni, the Bulgarian Diva-ta Zena), a fifth people; the Bulgarians row and variant were restored after verify because the people-table form "Bulgarian" was added after verify (phase 4b-peoples-3). The grade is unchanged.
Afanasyev records the dziwozony of Poland and the divé ženy of Bohemia.
Afanasyev records Czech belief that the divé ženy substitute unbaptised infants and harm women in childbed.

Afanasyev's two volumes count as one source; on these pages he draws on Siemieński and Wagilewicz, not on Machal, and Machal's Wild Women passage cites no source, so Machal and Afanasyev are counted as two independent sources for Czechs and Poles.
Erben is marked literary in the manifest; his note on the noon divé ženy is kept but not counted toward independence.
